On their father's death, on his own volition, Raja Ajit Chand carved out the state of Handur for his younger brother Sujit Chand and made him an independent ruler of Nalagarh (Handur) state. Shringar Chand went to war with the ruler of Kangra in which the former was victorious. He annexed with his state the Kangra territories of Mahal Mori and Tatwal. The Raja had ten sons, seven of whom were the ancestors of many Chandela Rajput families who also held jagirs. Shringar Chand's second son, Kailke, who had settled in village Darhol near Anandpur, belongs to the Chandela family of Ramgarh near Panchkula in Haryana. Later, the succeeding families shifted to Beri on the west bank of the Sutlej, opposite Bilaspur town and named it Beri Darol.

Before proceeding further, it is desirable to describe in brief the historical backdrop of the neighbouring Kangra. The ancient Kangra fort crowns a precipitous rock that dominates the surrounding area. It is surrounded on three sides by inaccessible cliffs and because of its strong position and massive walls, the fort was considered impregnable. Since ancient times, in the near proximity, the flame of jwalamukhi had been drawing people from far and wide to worship. Immense wealth had accumulated at the shrine. The deity commanded so much reverence and faith that the inmates took no care for its protection until Mahmud Chazni attacked it in c.1009. The entire treasury of the deity, Jwalamukhi was always kept inside Kangra fort, which was without a garrison or defence. The priests parleyed for sometime against Ghazni's attack but on the third day, they offered to surrender and opened the gates of the fort. A huge booty fell into the hands of the invaders, which is said to have amounted to 700,000 gold dinars, 700 mounds of gold and silver plates, 200 mounds of pure gold in ingots, 200 mounds of silver and 20 mounds of jewels including pearls, corals, diamonds and rubies. On his return, Mahmud Ghazni displayed the wealth piled on carpets in the courtyard of his palace to the wondering eyes of his subjects. Mohammed-binTughlaq conquered Nagarkot (Nagarkot was the name of the townand Kangra of the fort) in 1337. Around 1044, Mahipal, the Raja of Delhi, reoccupied Kangra, but the Raja of Kangra ventured to retake it in 1351. Alarmed at this, Firozshah Tughlak marched to Kangra. The Raja stood siege for sometime and then surrendered. Firoz's Nagarkot campaign was interesting-he caused 300 volumes of Sanskrit books preserved in the temple of Jwalamukbi to be rendered into Persian verse under the title of Dalal-il-l-Firuz Shahi by a court poet named Aazz-ud-din Khalid khan.

Dip Chand was the contemporary of Mughal emperor, Aurangzeb. When the emperor came to Lahore, he found that the Pathans of North West Frontier had badly defeated the Mughal army. He called Raja Dip Chand. On the request from the emperor, Dip Chand led an expedition of Kehloor army against the Pathans in which he was mainly assisted by his minister who also happened to be his cousin, Abhai Ram (ancestor of Chandel family of Bhadrog). Dip Chand was also accompanied by the troops of the neighbouring Ranas and Rais. Whilst his artillery thundered over the fort of Attock on the bank of the Indus, the troops overpowered the entire valley. Heavy casualties of enemy created panic. Fearing annihilation, the Pathans hoisted a white flag and surrendered. The entire Attock territory was won over. The success was significant. Attock¹ had been wrested from Raja Jaipal in 1002 by Mahmud Ghazni and since then it had remained in foreign hands. Its capture meant the liberation of northern India from the Pathans and Afghans. Aurangzeb was extremely happy when the news of this victory reached Lahore. At this glorious success, the emperor presented Raja Dip Chand with a purse of five lakh rupees, an army flag with an emblem of Hanuman and conferred on the Raja the title of Raja-e-Rajgan (king of kings). He also re-endorsed his supremacy and suzerainty over the twenty-two states—eleven on either side of the river Ravi-including important states of Jammu, Kangra, Mandi, Suket, Chamba, Guler, Kullu, Kutlehar, Datarpur, Siba, Jasrot, Bhandral, Bhadrawah, Chanheni and Mankot. Feroz Shah Tughlak had earlier bestowed a similar honour upon Raja Ratan Chand in the fifteenth century, which was later re-confirmed by Ibrahim Lodhi on Raja Uttam Chand. Kehloor was already the overlord of Twelve Thakurain in the Simla regions. With the new addition of twenty-two states, Kehloor became the head of thirty-four principalities, the highest honour ever earned by any single hill state. Unfortunately, Raja Dip Chand's glory was short lived. On his way back from Lahore, he was poisoned at Nadaun through the treachery of Raja Alam Chand of Kangra. His minister, Abhai Ram, tried to revive the Raja but all his efforts failed and Raja Dip Chand died. He was cremated at Nadaun on the bank of the Beas. Raja Dip Chand passed an order that in future, jaideva should be wished and addressed only to the Raja and jai to the Mians. Any refusal to obey. involved loss of their jagirs. All the Mians agreed to comply. At the same time, the salutation of Ram Ram was fixed for the Ranas. The heir apparent in former times used to bear the title of Yuvraj. It fell into disuse in the hills and the title of Tikka took its place. The title of Mian is of Mohammadan origin and is said to have been conferred by Jehangir on the young princes from the hills who were kept as hostages at his court. Feud with Guru Gobind Singh

Raja Bhim Chand, during his reign, was in constant feud2 with the Sikh guru, Gobind Singhji (born on December 22, 1666). Raja Kalyan Chand had earlier gifted two villages of Kiratpur and Kalyanpur to the sixth guru, Hargobind Singh, which continued to be in the possession of Guru Gobind Singh also. At the beginning, the Guruji and Raja Bhim Chand had cordial relations but the ties were strained between the two when the latter requested the guru to send his white elephant that was gifted to him by Raja Ram Rai of Assam. Bhim Chand wanted his son, Ajmer Chand, the would-be groom, to ride this elephant during his marriage with the daughter of Raja Fateh Shah of Garhwal, but the guru refused to accede to the request. Raja Bhim Chand was furious and asked Guru Gobind Singh to vacate the territory of Makhowal (later named as Anand Sahib), which the Raja claimed to have belonged to Bilaspur, failing which, to be ready for a fight. Guru Gobind Singh refuted the claim on the ground that the land in question had actually been purchased. Therefore, it had remained in full ownership of the gurus ever since. When Raja Medini Parkash of Sirmaur heard of the strife between the guru and the Raja of Bilaspur, he readily offered the former all the hospitality and arrangements for permanent stay and settlement in his state. Thereupon, at the advice of Mata Gujri, the guru migrated to Nahan and then came to Paonta Sahib and camped there. This place was fortified in 1685. Men and material further strengthened the garrison. Five hundred Pathan soldiers, earlier retired from Bassi-Pathana, joined the service of the guru. Another detachment of 500 Udasi disciples headed by Mahant Kripal Dass of Ludhiana reached the garrison for military training. Fearing the increasing military might of the guru, Raja Fateh Shah of Garhwal tried to win him over and sent precious presents and invited him to attend the marriage of his daughter. In return, the guru detailed Bhai Nand Chand with 500 soldiers and a detachment of a cavalry to attend the marriage ceremony and also sent gifts to the bride worth Rs. 1.25 lakh. The entourage was received warmly by the Raja and a special campsite for the stay was allotted to them. In the meanwhile, Raja Bhim Chand along with the barat was on the way to Srinagar (Garhwal). Raja Kripal of Kangra, Raja Kesri Chand of Jaswal, Raja Hari Chand of Handur, Raja Prithi Chand of Dhadwal, Raja Sukh Dyal of Jasrot and Rajas of Mandi and Suket accompanied the marriage entourage. A considerable armed force escorted the procession. When Guru Gobind Singh came to know of the arriving barat along with the military force, he sent a force of 500 men and blocked the route of the barat. The other alternate route was too long to reach Srinagar in time. Bhim Chand did not want to undertake a fight at such an auspicious occasion. He, therefore, sent his wazir to meet the guru and requested him to allow the barat to proceed further as the time for the lagan was approaching fast, but the guru refused. Thereupon, the Raja requested Guru Gobind Singh to at least allow the bridegroom and a few more persons to proceed so that the marriage ceremony would take place at the pre-fixed time, the rest of the barat would take another alternate route. To this, the guru finally agreed. When, on arrival at Srinagar, Bhim Chand came to know of the presence of Bhai Nand Chand along with the guru's force stationed at the nearby camp, a letter of expressed protest was sent to Raja Fateh Shah, the bride's father. Fateh Shah also barat and resentment at the guru's action of blocking the route of the an attack returned the presents sent by the guru. Nand Chand sensed on his forces and quietly withdrew from the scene and reported to the guru about the developments. The guru felt humiliated. When the marriage party was returning, a battle between the forces of the guru and Raja Bhim Chand took place in the year 1686 at Bhangani, a village near Paonta Sahib situated between the rivers Yamuna and Giri. As Raja Kripal Chand of Kangra, Raja Kesri Chand Jaswal, Raja Sukhdev Chand Jasrotia, Raja Hari Chand Handuria, Raja Prithi Chand Dadwalia were all accompanying the barat, therefore, they all were engaged in the battle in which, the Rajas of Handur, Jaswal and Jasrot were killed. It appears that bitterness between the two was also as a result of interference by the mercenary Pathan soldiers who had joined the guru's army after they had deserted the Mughal forces. These Pathans were repeatedly harassing the hill people.
